title: How to Give Your Kids $1 Million Each! (And It Won't Cost You a Cent)
author: Ashley Ormond
summary:
Ashley Ormond, a finance industry veteran with decades of experience in banking, capital markets, and investment, wrote *How to Give Your Kids $1 Million Each!* to address a specific, emotionally resonant problem: parents want to give their children a real financial head start, but most feel they don't earn enough to make a meaningful difference. Ormond's answer is that the size of the eventual gift matters less than the length of time compound returns are allowed to work — and that starting small, early, and consistently can turn a trivial daily amount into a seven-figure sum by the time a child reaches adulthood.

The book's plan, in its simplest form, involves opening an investment account for a child at birth, contributing a small, steadily increasing amount each month, and directing that money into low-cost, tax-effective investments — primarily company shares and, in later chapters, property — left largely untouched to compound over roughly twenty to twenty-five years. Ormond walks through the arithmetic in detail, showing how a starting contribution as small as around $31 per month, increased by a modest percentage each year to keep pace with inflation, can realistically grow to around $1 million by the time a child turns twenty-one or twenty-five, assuming historically reasonable long-term investment returns.

Structurally, the book follows a deliberate four-part "On your marks, Get ready, Get set, Go!" framing, moving the reader from understanding the core idea, to finding the spare dollar a day required to start, to the investment basics needed to execute the plan competently, to the specific asset classes (shares and property) used to build the fund. Ormond is careful throughout to stress that this is not a get-rich-quick scheme, a trading system, or a complex financial product — it depends on unglamorous, disciplined, low-cost investing sustained over two decades, with roughly an hour a month of actual attention required once it's set up.

The later chapters address two practical questions many parents overlook: how the plan behaves in years when investment returns disappoint, and how and when to actually hand the accumulated fund over to a now-adult child in a way that supports rather than undermines their financial maturity. Ormond closes by reframing the book's promise: that the deepest gift here isn't really the eventual dollar figure, but the financial literacy and habits a family builds together over the two decades it takes to get there, and the discipline of teaching children how to understand, protect, and grow money rather than simply handing them a windfall.

sections.title: Giving Your Kids $1 Million Each
sections.summary:
This opening chapter introduces the book's central promise and the basic mechanics behind it, establishing why a modest starting contribution can plausibly grow into $1 million over roughly two decades. Ormond's purpose here is to make the plan feel achievable rather than fantastical to a reader who assumes such an outcome requires substantial wealth.

He walks through the core plan: starting with as little as $1 in an account at a child's birth, contributing roughly $31 per month, and increasing that contribution by about 3 per cent annually to keep pace with inflation, all invested to target an average return around 11 per cent per year over the long term. Ormond presents a table showing how the fund grows over time under these assumptions, while being explicit that actual year-to-year returns will vary considerably and that the number is an approximate long-term outcome, not a guarantee.

The chapter closes by acknowledging that many readers will want to reach the target faster or aim higher, and points ahead to later chapters (on finding money to invest, and on shares and property specifically) where these variations are addressed in more detail.
keyLessons: A relatively small, steadily increasing monthly contribution, sustained for two decades, can plausibly compound into a seven-figure sum.
The plan depends on long-term average returns, which will vary significantly year to year even if the long-run average holds.
Framing a big number as a percentage of a small daily amount makes an ambitious goal feel achievable rather than abstract.

sections.title: Finding $1 per Day
sections.summary:
This chapter addresses the practical first obstacle most parents raise: where the money to start actually comes from. Its purpose is to make the case that the plan's starting contribution is genuinely within reach for most households, not just financially comfortable ones.

Ormond walks through concrete strategies for freeing up a small, consistent amount each month — reviewing discretionary spending, redirecting money from small recurring expenses, and treating the contribution as a fixed, non-negotiable line item similar to a bill rather than a discretionary extra that gets skipped in a tight month. He emphasizes that the amount needed to start is deliberately small precisely so that the barrier to beginning is minimized.

The chapter closes by transitioning into the mechanics of actually setting up the investment vehicle and account structure, which the following chapter addresses in more detail.
keyLessons: Treating the monthly contribution as a fixed, non-negotiable commitment (like a bill) protects the plan from being skipped during tight months.
The plan's starting contribution is deliberately small to minimize the barrier to actually beginning.
Reviewing small recurring discretionary expenses is often enough to free up the required monthly amount.

sections.title: Getting Started
sections.summary:
This chapter covers the practical steps of actually setting up the plan: choosing an account structure, understanding relevant tax considerations for investments held for or by a child, and establishing the discipline of regular contributions. Its purpose is to move the reader from concept to action.

Ormond discusses the administrative and tax dimensions of investing on behalf of a child in the Australian context, including account ownership structures and how earnings may be taxed differently depending on how the investment is held. He stresses the importance of automating contributions wherever possible so the plan doesn't depend on remembering to act each month.

The chapter closes by pointing toward the investment basics needed to actually choose where the money goes, setting up the next chapter's more foundational discussion of investing principles.
keyLessons: Account structure and tax treatment materially affect how much of the fund's growth is retained, and are worth understanding before starting.
Automating monthly contributions removes reliance on memory or willpower to sustain the plan over two decades.
Getting started with the right structure early avoids costly restructuring later in the plan's life.

sections.title: Investment Basics
sections.summary:
This chapter lays the foundational investing knowledge the rest of the book builds on, covering concepts like compound returns, diversification, risk versus return, and the difference between growth and income-generating investments. Its purpose is to ensure readers can evaluate the specific asset classes covered in later chapters with real understanding rather than blind trust.

Ormond explains why compounding requires time more than it requires large sums, why costs and fees matter disproportionately over a multi-decade horizon, and why a long time horizon changes the appropriate risk tolerance for a child's investment fund compared to, say, a retiree's portfolio. He keeps the explanations accessible, aimed at parents without a finance background rather than experienced investors.

The chapter closes by transitioning into the book's specific asset class chapters — first shares, then property — applying these foundational principles to real investment choices.
keyLessons: Compounding depends far more on time than on the size of the initial contribution.
Fees and costs compound negatively over a multi-decade horizon just as returns compound positively, and deserve serious scrutiny.
A long time horizon (two decades or more) justifies a different risk tolerance than a shorter-term investment goal would.

sections.title: Company Shares
sections.summary:
This chapter covers the first of the two main asset classes Ormond recommends for the plan: listed company shares, typically via low-cost, diversified vehicles. Its purpose is to give parents enough understanding to select and hold share investments appropriately for a multi-decade child's fund.

He discusses the historical long-term return characteristics of share markets, the importance of diversification across companies and sectors rather than picking individual stocks, and the discipline of staying invested through market downturns rather than reacting to short-term volatility — a discipline Ormond argues is easier to maintain with a genuinely long time horizon like a child's fund.

The chapter closes by turning to property as a second, complementary asset class covered in the next chapter, positioning shares and property together as the two main building blocks of the plan.
keyLessons: Diversified exposure to shares, rather than individual stock-picking, suits a long-term, low-maintenance family investment plan.
Staying invested through market downturns is easier to sustain with a genuinely long time horizon.
Share markets have historically delivered strong long-term average returns, though with significant year-to-year variability.

sections.title: Property Investments
sections.summary:
This chapter covers the second core asset class, real estate, discussing how and when property might be incorporated into the child's investment plan alongside or instead of shares. Its purpose is to give parents a balanced view of property's role in a long-term, low-cost investment strategy.

Ormond discusses the practical considerations of property investment — larger capital requirements, illiquidity, ongoing costs, and the use of leverage — contrasting these with the simpler, more liquid, and lower-cost nature of share investing covered in the previous chapter. He offers guidance on how a family might combine both asset classes, or choose one over the other, depending on their circumstances and risk tolerance.

The chapter closes by moving into the book's chapter on how the combined fund actually grows and behaves over the full multi-decade period, addressing the real-world variability the earlier chapters' idealized projections leave out.
keyLessons: Property investment involves larger capital requirements, illiquidity, and ongoing costs that differ meaningfully from share investing.
Leverage can amplify property returns but also amplifies risk, requiring careful consideration within a long-term family plan.
Shares and property can be combined or chosen selectively depending on a family's circumstances and risk tolerance.

sections.title: How the Fund Grows Over Time
sections.summary:
This chapter addresses the realistic, non-linear path a child's investment fund is likely to take over two decades, directly confronting the idealized straight-line projections used earlier in the book. Its purpose is to prepare parents for the emotional and practical experience of investing through good years and bad.

Ormond walks through how sequences of strong and weak investment years affect the fund's trajectory differently depending on when they occur, and stresses that periods of decline are a normal, expected part of a multi-decade investment plan rather than a sign that the plan has failed. He offers guidance on how parents should (and should not) respond during downturns, generally counseling patience and continued contributions rather than panic or withdrawal.

The chapter closes by turning to the plan's endpoint — actually handing the fund over to the now-adult child — which the next and final chapter addresses.
keyLessons: A multi-decade investment fund will experience real periods of decline; this is normal and does not indicate the plan has failed.
The timing of strong and weak return years, not just their average, affects the fund's final trajectory.
Continuing contributions through downturns, rather than pausing or withdrawing, is generally the more effective long-term response.

sections.title: Handing the Plan Over to the Kids
sections.summary:
The book's closing substantive chapter addresses the practical and emotional question of how and when to transfer the accumulated fund to a child who has become an adult. Its purpose is to ensure the money supports rather than undermines the child's financial maturity.

Ormond discusses the risks of handing over a large lump sum to a young adult without preparation, and argues for gradually involving the child in understanding and eventually managing the fund well before the formal handover, so that financial literacy is transferred alongside the money itself. He offers considerations around timing the handover (a fixed age, a milestone, or a gradual transition) and connects this back to the book's broader theme that the real gift is as much about capability as about capital.

The chapter, and the book, close by reiterating that the plan's ultimate purpose is to give children both a financial foundation and the knowledge to protect and grow it themselves.
keyLessons: Handing over a large lump sum without prior financial education creates real risk of the fund being poorly managed or quickly depleted.
Gradually involving a child in understanding the fund before the formal handover builds the capability needed to manage it well.
The timing and structure of the handover deserves as much deliberate planning as the investment strategy itself.
Start a child's investment fund as early as possible; time, not the size of the initial contribution, drives most of the eventual outcome.
Treat the monthly contribution as a fixed, non-negotiable commitment rather than a discretionary expense.
Understand account structure and tax treatment before starting, since they materially affect long-term outcomes.
Favor diversified, low-cost investments over individual stock-picking or complex products for a multi-decade family plan.
Expect and plan for real periods of investment decline; continue contributions through downturns rather than reacting to short-term volatility.
Combine or choose between shares and property deliberately based on your family's capital, risk tolerance, and liquidity needs.
Automate contributions so the plan doesn't depend on remembering to act each month for twenty years.
Prepare a child for eventually managing the fund by involving them in understanding it well before the formal handover.

conceptsFrameworks.name: The $1-a-Day Compounding Plan
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Ormond's core framework: starting an investment fund for a child at birth with a very small initial contribution (around $31 per month, roughly equivalent to $1 per day), increased modestly each year for inflation, and invested for long-term growth over roughly two decades to realistically reach a target of around $1 million by early adulthood.

conceptsFrameworks.name: On Your Marks, Get Ready, Get Set, Go!
conceptsFrameworks.definition: The book's four-part organizing structure, moving the reader from understanding the core plan (On your marks), to finding the money to start (Get ready), to acquiring the investment knowledge needed to execute it (Get set), to actually implementing it through shares and property (Go!).

actionSteps: Calculate a realistic small monthly amount you could commit to a child's investment fund starting this month, and set it up as an automatic, non-negotiable transfer.
Review your current discretionary spending for one week and identify a specific recurring expense you could redirect toward this plan.
Research the tax-effective account structures available in your country for investing on behalf of a minor before opening an account.
Decide, in writing, how you'll respond during a future market downturn (continue contributions, avoid checking the balance daily, etc.) before it actually happens.
If you already have a plan running, schedule a yearly one-hour review to increase the contribution in line with inflation and check the account structure still makes sense.
reflectionQuestions: What's actually stopping you from starting a plan like this today — the amount required, or the belief that a small amount couldn't possibly matter?
How would you want your own child to be involved in understanding this fund as they grow older, and at what age?
What would it mean for your family if the real value of this plan turned out to be the financial habits built along the way, rather than the final number?

points: The plan's headline $1 million outcome depends on an assumed average annual return around 11 per cent sustained over roughly two decades; this is higher than many long-term conservative return assumptions used by financial planners, and actual results could fall well short if long-run market returns are lower than assumed.

The book is written specifically for the Australian tax, account, and investment environment (including references to structures like the historical "baby bonus"), so international readers will need to adapt or substitute the tax and account guidance for their own jurisdiction.

Ormond's illustrative example of a reader starting with government baby-bonus money and cutting expenses like smoking to fund contributions makes the plan sound broadly accessible, but doesn't fully engage with households facing genuine financial precarity for whom even a small fixed monthly commitment may not be realistic.

The book's core arithmetic assumes uninterrupted contributions for roughly two decades; it offers guidance on continuing through market downturns but less extensive treatment of what happens to the plan's outcome if contributions are paused or reduced during a family financial crisis.

As with any long-horizon compounding illustration, the dramatic-sounding final figure is sensitive to the specific assumed rate of return, and small changes in that assumption compound into very large differences in the projected outcome by year twenty.
criticalTake.contextNote: First published in 2006 and revised in 2011, the book's specific references (like the government "baby bonus") reflect Australian policy settings from that period that have since changed, so readers should verify current equivalent programs and tax rules rather than relying on the book's specific figures.

whoThisIsFor: Parents or grandparents in Australia (or a similar tax environment) looking for a low-cost, long-term, low-maintenance way to build a meaningful investment fund for a child.
whenToReadThis: Read it as early as possible in a child's life — ideally around birth — since the plan's outcome depends heavily on the number of years compounding is allowed to work.

authorBio.name: Ashley Ormond
authorBio.bio:
Ashley Ormond spent 25 years in the finance industry, including senior executive roles at major international banking and finance groups, and has served as a director of listed, private, charitable, and not-for-profit organisations. He holds degrees in economic history, law, and finance, and is a CFA charter-holder.

Ormond has lectured on capital markets for the Securities Institute of Australia (later FINSIA) and for CFA Institute courses, and has been a regular media commentator and conference speaker on financial topics. His professional background in institutional finance underpins the book's emphasis on low-cost, disciplined, long-horizon investing rather than speculative or complex strategies.

*How to Give Your Kids $1 Million Each!* became an Australian bestseller and was revised and updated in a second edition, reflecting continued reader interest in its long-term family investment approach.
